**On the human's position:** The maintainer's words (Q3, park): "all I have to do is push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice." Three attacks. First, "juice" is asserted, not measured: the vendor's own pages say Fable 5 and Opus 5 prompts "should perform well without changes" on their successors, and the strongest-model ablation (2609.20804) puts process prose at -2.0 to -0.4%. The profile shipped in PR #78 without a with/without run, and `claude plugin eval` (v2.1.269, 3 runs against a no-plugin baseline) has existed since 2026-09-11 to get that number. Second, "push to an update" already works: the profile is `vendor` kind (install-manifest.ts:30), PR #78 delivered it through `update`, and the parked feature's spec 3 swaps the row. The bottleneck is the maintainer's hours condensing a 6,610-word page by hand, not a delivery mechanism, and fetch only buys between-release freshness that the vendor says is low-value. Third, "everyone" is wrong for his own fleet: AGENTS.md:181-182 runs Codex on GPT-6 and Pi on kimi-k3, so two of his three harnesses have no Claude juice to receive, and D6 (model-profile.ts:20) already ships Fable steering to Pi regardless of the model it runs. One point supports his instinct against hand-written docs: the hand condensation dropped 'The user is not watching in real time' (profile:40-42), the sentence the guide says 'carries much of the effect. Keep it as written.' Hand editing introduced an error the vendor warned about. But the fix is verbatim vendor blocks behind a measurement, not a fetch pipeline that automates the same ungated condensation. Does my lens move his position? Yes, from 'park until the new system pushes guides' to 'park until a with/without Δ exists'. If the eval Δ is ~0, delete the profile and keep only the subtract audit in optimize Step 2c; if it is positive, ship verbatim dated vendor snapshots through `update` and skip live fetch entirely.

##### Solo dev on Pi, open-weight model — qualified

**Strongest refutation:** P5 conflates delivery with content. The thing that helps a coding agent is the condensed, model-tagged profile (1,267 words, docs/templates/reference/model-profile-claude-fable-5-1.md), not the vendor page: the live Fable 5.1 Markdown is 6,610 words and most of its body is API-integration material (append-only history, prefix_mismatch_behavior, prompt-cache, thinking blocks, effort parameter; fetched 2026-09-24). Someone still has to decide which sections apply, which the parked Opus 5.5 brief did by hand (4 of 11 sections "Act", 5 "Not applicable"). That decision IS a per-model doc; fetching only changes where its raw material comes from. For my model the mechanism has nothing to fetch and nothing to subtract: Qwen model cards and Moonshot's docs publish sampling and reasoning_effort guidance, not behavioral steering or "remove this for older models" language (huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B README; platform.kimi.ai/docs/guide/prompt-best-practice.md; kimi-k3-quickstart.md, all fetched 2026-09-24). Worse, Joycraft already ships me the wrong vendor's profile: src/model-profile.ts:19-20 installs the Fable doc for 'pi' and 'omp' on the fable-native D6 rationale "Pi and omp users run Claude models" (docs/features/2026-09-22-fable-native-sdlc-harness/brief.md:33-37), while this machine's ~/.pi/agent/models-store.json lists kimi-k3, qwen3p8-max, deepseek-v4-pro and glm-5p3 under moonshotai, deepseek and fireworks providers. Pi 0.80.10's dist/core/system-prompt.js (109 lines) never references the model, so the parked brief's fallback rule "apply every block tagged for any current Claude model" would apply Anthropic's steering to a Qwen run. Fetch-and-subtract keyed to a Claude URL makes that worse, not better. Finally the "Codex precedent" is misread in shape: Codex hits one stable resolver URL, treats returned guide URLs "as opaque: fetch those exact URLs without deriving, substituting, or appending", and its bundled latest-model.md calls itself "a compact, non-authoritative fallback" with no date (codex-rs/skills/src/assets/samples/openai-docs/references/model-migration.md:30, latest-model.md:3, fetched 2026-09-24). Anthropic offers no resolver, only llms.txt; its docs moved docs.anthropic.com -> docs.claude.com -> platform.claude.com and renamed claude-4-best-practices to claude-prompting-best-practices (all redirect to 200 today; prompting-claude-opus-4-6.md is 404). Stability is "redirects have held so far", not a contract.

**Qualification:** P5 survives only as: (1) fetch at `update` time (already online for npm; src/update-check.ts:97,328 is the existing fetch-with-cache-and-3s-deadline pattern), never at session start, where a 6,610-word page would cost a per-token API user roughly 5x the tokens of the condensed profile every session; (2) the fetched page is raw material for a condensation pass whose output stays a short profile with `Applies to:` tags per block (the parked D1 shape), and that condensed doc, dated, is what installs and what the bundled fallback is; (3) the profile install is keyed to the actual running model read from the harness config (Pi models.json / session model, Claude Code's system prompt), not to the harness as src/model-profile.ts:20 does today; open-weight and unknown models get no vendor profile, or an explicit "no vendor guidance; keep scaffolding" stub, never Claude's; (4) Anthropic discovery goes through platform.claude.com/llms.txt with redirects followed, OpenAI through the latest-model resolver, and both fall back to the dated bundle when the fetch fails or the slug 404s; (5) the subtract step stays the existing optimize Step 2c audit (src/skills/joycraft-optimize.md:74-84, RETIRE/PROBATION, advisory) and tune's `probation:` model comment, which need a profile with stable headings, not a fetch.

**On the human's position:** Q3, verbatim: \"all I have to do is push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice.\" That push already exists and needs no fetch: the profile is a vendor-owned template (src/model-profile.ts:14; ownership kind vendor in src/install-manifest.ts), so bumping the template and releasing makes the next `update` replace it, backing up edited copies under docs/.joycraft/local/replaced/. What the sentence hides is the word \"everyone\". On my lens \"everyone gets the new juice\" means a Pi user on Kimi K3 or Qwen 3.8 gets Anthropic's Fable steering, because D6 keyed the install to the harness on the false premise that Pi users run Claude models (brief.md:33-37) and Pi cannot tell the skill what model is running. The push mechanism is fine; the content must be keyed to the model actually running, and for my model the honest content is \"no vendor guidance exists; keep the scaffolding\", which the inverted-U result supports. My lens moves the position from \"push the guide\" to \"push a condensed, dated, model-tagged profile, installed only where the running model matches, with nothing Claude-shaped landing on open-weight runs.\" On the Park decision itself: the parked D1 (one Claude doc, Applies-to tags) and spec 5 (Pi loop appends the fenced block via --append-system-prompt) are the right shape for Claude-on-Pi and the wrong shape for open-weight-on-Pi unless spec 5 checks the model first; the park is defensible, but \"it may become moot\" is not the reason. Fetch does not make hand-condensation moot; it only changes the input to it.

##### Evidence auditor — qualified

**Strongest refutation:** The citations P5 rests on all hold, but the argument built on them does not. (1) The one named precedent is misapplied: Codex's openai-docs skill (codex-rs/skills/src/assets/samples/openai-docs/SKILL.md, fetched 2026-09-24, line 36: "Use references/latest-model.md only as a disclosed fallback") is a documentation-lookup skill that answers user questions about OpenAI docs; it does not fetch model guidance to steer the agent. Codex's actual per-model steering is bundled models.json (~60KB per GPT-6 model, pack §6.3), i.e. vendor-authored per-model docs shipped by release, which is the thing P5 says to abandon. Its open issue #43164 (2026-09-06) shows fetch-first breaking offline users. (2) The fetched artifact is not a profile. Live word counts match the pack to the digit: Fable 5.1 6,610 words, Opus 5.5 3,969, best practices 8,013, migration guides 9,399 and 9,330. Of the Fable 5.1 guide's 16 H2 sections (fetched), about ten are API-only or off Joycraft's surface (effort levels, xhigh/max long outputs, vision crop/zoom, search triggering, safeguard false positives, lead-agent/subagent timing); the parked Opus 5.5 brief's own table scores 4 act / 2 handled by Claude Code / 5 not applicable. The pack's own inference (§6) concedes "the useful step is condensing a 2–9k-word vendor page into a ~1,000-word profile." Condensing is per-model authoring. Fetch removes the delivery step, not the labor, and the labor is where the value is. (3) "Static falls months behind" is Aider's number (5 months, §6.3), not Joycraft's. Joycraft tags: v0.7.11 09-03, v0.7.12 09-03, v0.7.13 09-06, v0.7.15 09-07, v0.7.16 09-23; the Fable 5.1 profile shipped 22 days after the 09-01 guide, and the Opus 5.5 feature was decomposed within two days of the 09-22 release. Joycraft's release cadence already matches Anthropic's ~3-week guide cadence, so the currency problem the fetch solves is not measured in this repo. (4) The maintainer's "push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice" is what the current design does: the profile is a vendor-owned template (docs/templates/reference/model-profile-claude-fable-5-1.md, ownership kind vendor per src/install-manifest.ts:30 as summarized in §8.8), replaced on `npx joycraft update` with a backup; PR #78 delivered it that way. Fetch adds nothing to "push to update." What survives is the subtract half: every vendor quote about removing stale instructions verified verbatim.

**Qualification:** P5 survives only as: bundled, condensed, versioned per-model profile delivered by `joycraft update` (today's mechanism) plus a subtract audit in optimize (vendor quotes verified), with fetch used strictly as a change detector against platform.claude.com/llms.txt and developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latest-model.md that follows redirects, never constructs slugs for models not listed, and never places fetched vendor text into agent context unsummarized. The 'fetch beats per-model docs' framing is refuted; the 'subtract' framing stands.

### P6 — Jev routing on the hot path as a core part of the product

**Ruling: FLIP.** The maintainer's override — Jev routing prompts to skills, files, context-map pointers, and tool calls on the hot path, as a core part of the product, for anyone who brings a key — does not stand. It is replaced by: Jev ships as an opt-in, bring-your-own-key advisory judge off the hot path (doc ranking, report-claim verification over code-filtered state), plus a shadow-mode skill router that logs its pick beside the skill actually used; nothing touches the prompt path until an eval on Joycraft's own roster, with real prompts, shows Jev beating the model-free baselines, and files, context-map pointers, and tool calls stay out until each has its own measurement.

**Claim as argued:** The maintainer overrode the lead's advisory-first recommendation: Jev (TypeSafe) should route prompts to skills, files, context-map pointers, and tool calls on the hot path for anyone who brings a key, as a core part of the product, degrading to today's behavior when unreachable. Skeptic angles: the only routing evidence used 60-char descriptions and easy synthetic requests; a model-free forced-eval hook hit 22/22 with no false positives; hooks fail open; Jev reads literally and adversarial text moves its answer; hosted-only, US-only, no SLA, incidents on two of the last four days; per-user keys only under TypeSafe's terms; a zero-dependency CLI acquiring a hosted dependency on every prompt. The maintainer says it is "insanely good and basically free" in their own projects and is "open to the skeptics saying no."

**Replacement claim:** Jev is an optional, off-by-default, per-key advisory judge in Joycraft — off the hot path first (doc ranking, claim verification), shadow-logged as a skill router second — and becomes a hot-path router for skills only after a held-out eval on Joycraft's 22-skill roster with frontier agents beats the model-free forced-eval and disable-model-invocation baselines. It is never "core": a hosted, AS-IS, no-SLA dependency with recent latency incidents cannot be a product default, and file, context-map, and tool-call routing have no evidence anywhere.

**Condition:** Not a qualify ruling, but the exact path that revives a narrower P6 (all required): (a) a held-out invocation eval on Joycraft's actual roster (22 skills, or the post-P1 hub) with Fable 5.1 / Opus 5.5 as the agent and a Pi open-weight arm, using real prompts pulled from `joycraft telemetry` transcripts and labeled with the intended skill or "none", not prompts authored from the skills' own descriptions; (b) three arms — native description matching, disable-model-invocation on the 11 agent-entry skills plus a model-free forced-eval router block, and jev-1.13 — with Jev winning on wrong-load minus break-rate and on no-skill prompts; (c) any hot-path adapter carries its own client timeout of at most 2 s (the hook `timeout` field is settable) so a latency incident costs 2 s, not the 30 s default; (d) enabled per project on teams, not per developer, with every routing decision, confidence, and fallback written to the telemetry store; (e) TypeSafe confirms in writing that a developer running Joycraft's hook under their own key is an application "developed and operated by Customer" under the 2026-09-23 MCA; (f) skills only — files, context-map pointers, and tool calls stay off the hot path until each has its own eval.

**Judge's reasoning:** Four skeptics returned refuted and one (solo-pi) returned qualified, and the qualified return concedes the load-bearing words: "'Core part of the product' is refuted; 'an opt-in adapter that may help my model class' is not." So the panel is unanimous that "core" and "hot path" fail and disagrees only on what survives.

The proposition rests on one measurement and one anecdote. The measurement is TypeSafe's skill_suggestion cookbook, which every skeptic re-fetched and confirmed verbatim: Haiku 4.5 as agent, 182 skills, descriptions cut to 60 chars (Hermes's default, not TypeSafe's), 488 synthetic requests written by Sonnet 5 from each skill's own SKILL.md that the cookbook itself calls "easier than the ones users send", run on jev-1.12, thresholds tuned in-sample, wrong loads 16.8% to 7.3%, 37 fixed and 7 broken, and a conclusion the vendor scopes to "when an agent of yours carries a large roster". I verified the repo side: Joycraft has 22 skills with full descriptions totalling 3,619 chars (81 to 223 each), under the 8k listing budget, targeting frontier agents, with zero invocation evals (check.sh cannot assert which skill ran) and zero Jev references in src/, templates/, or scripts/. The regime does not transfer: the roster is 8x smaller, the descriptions 2 to 4x longer, the agent stronger, and P1 proposes to collapse the roster further, which removes the problem the cookbook solved. The only third-party Claude Code build of that cookbook (shimo4228/jev-skill-router, solo-pi) got 3 wrong of 6 on a real session and its README says it is "unlikely to help a strong model as a router". Meanwhile a model-free forced-eval hook measured 22/22 with 0/5 false positives while a Haiku classifier hook fired wrongly on 4/5 non-matching prompts (Spence, 2026-02-08, small n but the only direct comparison), and nobody has run either baseline on Joycraft's roster.

The anecdote ("insanely good and basically free" in the maintainer's own projects) has no artifact, number, task shape, or agent model, and the vendor's own coding-agents page positions Jev inside applications the agent builds, "not a drop-in replacement for the LLM behind Claude Code". Good-in-apps, where code retrieves and filters then asks a typed question over small state, is the inverse of a UserPromptSubmit hook shipping an unfiltered prompt plus 22 descriptions plus the active queue every turn; jev-1.13's own jaggedness page says "Accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision" and prescribes "Retrieve and filter in code first".

Three of the four routing targets (files, context-map pointers, tool calls) have no measurement anywhere in the pack, the repo, or TypeSafe's docs. Context-map routing has one destination today (a single Context Map row) and the map is never regenerated. Tool-call gating via PreToolUse adds latency, fails open by Anthropic's own words ("don't count on a stalled hook to act as a gate"), and the gated agent writes the input the judge reads.

"Degrades to today's behavior when unreachable" covers only the hard-outage case. The status page I fetched shows the Sep 23 incidents were latency (3 min and 12 min), not downtime; a latency incident does not trip the fail-open path, it stalls every prompt for every keyed colleague until the hook timeout (30 s default, though settable). The MCA, updated the day before the panel, is AS IS and AS AVAILABLE with no uptime commitment, and the JS SDK broke compatibility four days after release.

"Basically free" is true in dollars (about $0.042/M input, roughly $0.02/session) and false in the currencies a harness pays: latency on every prompt, a second vendor account and key per user, per-harness adapter maintenance on TypeSafe's cadence as well as Anthropic's, config-patch plumbing to reach about 15 existing installs, and on teams (team-lead) a per-developer fork in exactly the layer the maintainer's own Q1 answer says must stay invariant, with telemetry that cannot attribute a skill on Codex (src/telemetry.ts:404, verified). The maintainer's own list of wins (files, context-map pointers, research, web scraping, panels) is mostly the off-hot-path advisory use the lead recommended; only "help claude code with tool calls" needs the hot path, and that is the use with the weakest evidence and strongest adversarial exposure.

Why flip rather than qualify: the claim as written asserts three things — core, hot path, per-key default — and the evidence inverts all three. The condition field records the path back, but that path is the lead's advisory-first shape, which is the position the maintainer overrode. Why flip rather than kill: solo-pi's point survives — the one measured gain is on a mid-tier agent, which is exactly the open-weight Pi user class, and the inverted-U predicts those users benefit most; and off-hot-path uses match Jev's documented strengths. So Jev has a place in Joycraft; it is not the place the proposition names.

**Strongest refutation considered:** The strongest case for keeping was assembled from the skeptics' own evidence_against lists: the measured routing win is real and large (wrong loads more than halved); dollar cost is negligible; Claude Code's http hook handler with allowedEnvVars makes a per-user-key adapter thin and keeps the key out of the repo; the hook timeout field is settable so the stall can be capped at 1 to 2 s rather than 30 s; fail-open is real, so the worst case is today's behavior; the "zero-dependency CLI" premise is overstated (commander is a runtime dependency and the CLI already calls the npm registry behind a deadline); BYOK fits the MCA's "developed and operated by Customer" reading; inputs are not used for training; the forced-eval alternative is itself slower (10.7 s vs 6.4 s per prompt) and is prompt injection every turn; and for mid-tier open-weight agents the inverted-U predicts a real gain. I considered this seriously and it does defeat the weaker skeptic angles (cost, dependency purity, licensing as a hard blocker). It does not defeat the central one: none of it produces a measurement of Joycraft's own mis-route rate or of Jev's delta over a model-free baseline on this roster, and none of it touches files, context-map pointers, or tool calls, for which no evidence exists at all. A settable 2 s timeout and a compliant key make a good opt-in experiment, not a core default.

- The only routing measurement was Haiku 4.5 over 182 skills with 60-char (Hermes-default) descriptions, 488 synthetic Sonnet-5-authored requests the cookbook calls 'easier than the ones users send', on jev-1.12 with in-sample thresholds; wrong loads 16.8%->7.3%, 37 fixed / 7 broken; conclusion scoped to 'a large roster'. — https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion.md, fetched 2026-09-24 by all five skeptics; all numbers confirmed verbatim
- Joycraft has 22 skills with full descriptions totalling 3,619 chars (81-223 each), zero disable-model-invocation, zero Jev/TypeSafe references anywhere in src/, templates/, scripts/, commander as sole runtime dependency, and no invocation evals. — Verified by me 2026-09-24: /Users/compiler/Developer/joycraft/src/skills/*.md, package.json, grep of src templates scripts; evidence pack §8.6

**What would change the ruling:** A held-out invocation eval on Joycraft's own roster would move this ruling to qualify or keep: real prompts from the telemetry scanner labeled with the intended skill or 'none', three arms (native, disable-model-invocation plus model-free forced-eval router block, jev-1.13) on Fable 5.1 / Opus 5.5 and on a Pi open-weight agent, with Jev beating the best model-free arm on wrong-load minus break-rate and on no-skill and adversarial prompts by a stated margin. Any measurement at all of Jev routing files, context-map pointers, or tool calls in a coding agent would revive those targets individually. A 60-day status-page window with zero latency incidents, or a self-hosted/zero-retention option available below enterprise tier, would weaken the hot-path reliability objection. Written confirmation from TypeSafe that BYOK harness use fits 'developed and operated by Customer' under the 2026-09-23 MCA would remove the licensing hedge. A shadow-mode log across the ~15 colleague installs showing Jev's pick agreeing with the skill actually used at a rate above native matching would be the cheapest single piece of evidence to change the ruling.

**Human position moved?** Yes. The maintainer's Q5 position — Jev routing on the hot path, core, for anyone who brings a key, overriding the lead's advisory-first recommendation — was moved by all five skeptics and by my own verification, back to the lead's shape with three additions. The evidence that moved it: (1) the only routing measurement does not transfer (Haiku 4.5, 182 skills, 60-char Hermes-default index, synthetic Sonnet-5-authored requests the vendor calls easier than real ones, jev-1.12, 7 regressions) and Joycraft's regime is the opposite (22 skills, full descriptions, frontier agents, verified in-repo); (2) 'insanely good' has no artifact — zero Jev references in the repo, no eval, no numbers, no agent model — and comes from in-app use, which the vendor's coding-agents page and jaggedness page say is the correct shape while a per-prompt hook over unfiltered state is the shape they warn against; (3) three of the four named targets (files, context-map pointers, tool calls) have no measurement anywhere, and the context map has one row; (4) 'basically free' is true in dollars and false in latency (two of the last three incidents on the status page I fetched were latency, which does not trip fail-open), in complexity (per-harness adapter, per-user key plumbing, config-patch to ~15 installs, a moving SDK), and on teams in review variance (per-developer forks in the layer the maintainer's own Q1 says stays fixed, with Codex skill attribution unavailable); (5) the maintainer's own list of wins is mostly the off-hot-path advisory uses. What was not moved: the instinct that a typed judge is useful where a check needs meaning, and solo-pi's observation that the evidence favors mid-tier open-weight agents — the Pi user class — more than the frontier setup the maintainer tests on. The maintainer said he is open to the skeptics saying no; on 'core' and 'hot path' and 'for anyone who brings a key', this is that no. On 'Jev in Joycraft at all', it is not.

#### Skeptics

##### Agent-harness expert — refuted

**Strongest refutation:** The only routing evidence fixes a problem Joycraft does not have. TypeSafe's cookbook improved skill selection for a 182-skill roster whose index Hermes truncates to 60 characters, in front of Haiku 4.5, on requests the cookbook itself says are "easier than the ones users send" — and it still left 7.3% wrong loads and broke 7 requests the agent had handled correctly alone (docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion.md, fetched 2026-09-24). Joycraft has 22 skills, full descriptions totalling 3,931 chars (~180 each, src/skills/*.md), frontier agents, and nobody has measured its baseline mis-route rate. Where someone did measure a Claude Code skill-activation problem (Sonnet 4.5, 22 prompts), a model-free forced-eval hook went 50-55% → 22/22 with 0/5 false positives, while the model-classifier hook fired wrongly on 4/5 non-matching prompts (scottspence.com, 2026-02-08). Jev's own jaggedness page says "Accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision… Retrieve and filter in code first, and send only the fields the question needs" — the exact opposite of a per-prompt hook that ships prompt + 22 descriptions + active queue every turn. Putting a hosted call with three latency incidents in the last five days (status.typesafe.ai: Sep 19 downtime 18 min, Sep 20, Sep 22, two on Sep 23) in front of every prompt, for a gain no one has measured on this roster, and calling it core, is how harnesses accrete: each added defense makes the system "less understandable while appearing more robust" (Ronacher, pack §1.8). "Degrades to today's behavior when unreachable" covers the easy failure (hard outage → fast error). It does not cover the two failures a hot-path hook actually suffers: elevated latency (no error, every prompt waits, up to the 30 s UserPromptSubmit cap) and confident wrong answers (7.3% wrong loads, 7 regressions, adversarial text "can move the answer"). "Tool call" routing via PreToolUse adds 0.1–0.3 s per edit, fails open by Anthropic's own words ("don't count on a stalled hook to act as a gate"), and the gated agent authors the input. "Context-map pointers" routing has one destination today (AGENTS.md:189-191, a single row).

**Qualification:** Not applicable to the verdict as stated (refuted). What would survive: Jev as an opt-in, BYOK, off-hot-path advisory judge (doc ranking, claim verification over code-filtered state ≤32k), shipped only after (a) disable-model-invocation on the 11 agent-entry skills and (b) a model-free forced-eval router are measured on Joycraft's own 22-skill roster with frontier agents, and Jev shows a delta over that baseline on a held-out prompt set that includes adversarial and no-skill prompts. Any hot-path adapter must carry its own sub-2 s client timeout, since the 30 s UserPromptSubmit cap is the only ceiling Claude Code provides.

**On the human's position:** The maintainer: "ive been using it in projects and it's insanely good and basically free… it will help route what files to look at, what pointers in the context map to look at, help claude code with tool calls… it should be core part of the product now but I'm open to the skeptics saying no." My lens moves this, on three points. (1) Where the experience comes from. Using Jev in your own projects means Jev as an application primitive: code retrieves and filters, then asks a typed question over a small state — exactly what TypeSafe's programming model and its jaggedness page prescribe ("Retrieve and filter in code first"). A UserPromptSubmit hook is the inverse: an unfiltered prompt plus 22 descriptions plus the active queue on every turn, in front of a frontier agent that TypeSafe itself says Jev is "not a drop-in replacement for". Good-in-apps does not transfer to good-as-harness-router; the one published harness-routing result had a 60-char, 182-skill, Haiku-class problem Joycraft does not have and still regressed 7 requests. (2) "Basically free." True in dollars; false in the two currencies a harness pays. Latency: three elevated-latency incidents in the last five days, and a latency incident does not trip the fail-open path, it slows every prompt for every colleague with a key. Complexity: a per-harness hook adapter, per-user key plumbing, a moving SDK (breaking change four days after release), and config-patch machinery to reach the ~15 existing installs — all on the hot path, all to be maintained on TypeSafe's cadence as well as Anthropic's. (3) The three named targets. "Pointers in the context map": one row exists (AGENTS.md:189-191) and the map is never regenerated, so there is nothing to route until P0/P1 rebuild the pointer layer. "What files to look at": Jev needs code to enumerate ≤255 candidates first; the retrieval is the hard part and Jev only reranks it. "Help with tool calls": PreToolUse adds 0.1–0.3 s per edit, fails open, and the agent writes the input the judge reads. What does survive the maintainer's own words is the instinct behind them: a typed judge is useful where a check needs meaning. That is the lead's advisory-first shape — opt-in, off the hot path (doc ranking, claim verification), measured against the model-free forced-eval and disable-model-invocation baselines before anything touches a prompt. The override should be reversed; the enthusiasm should be pointed at a measurement, not a default.

##### AI researcher — refuted

**Strongest refutation:** There is no measurement of the thing the proposition claims to fix, and the one measurement that exists comes from a regime that does not transfer. The skill-suggestion cookbook (docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion.md, fetched 2026-09-24) ran Haiku 4.5 over 182 Hermes skills with descriptions averaging 54 chars (max 60), on 488 synthetic single-turn prompts written by Sonnet 5 from the SKILL.md files, with the 0.30 gate/fit thresholds tuned on the same set and no held-out real-user prompts; the authors write that "the requests are easier than the ones users send." That is a deliberately starved baseline: a small agent, a roster 8x Joycraft's, descriptions 2–4x shorter than Joycraft's (79–221 chars, src/skills/*.md frontmatter; 3.3k total, under the 8k listing budget in claude-code#64606). Joycraft's condition is the opposite: 22 skills, full descriptions in budget, frontier agents (Fable 5.1 / Opus 5.5), and zero invocation evals (evidence pack §8.6: "No invocation evals; check.sh ... none checks which skill ran"). Even in the favorable regime Jev's residual wrong-load was 7.3% and it broke 7 of 488 requests the baseline got right; on a frontier model with 22 in-budget descriptions the native error rate is unmeasured and plausibly already near that residual, so a hot-path router can subtract as easily as add. The harness ablation (arxiv 2609.20804, 2026-09-17: "Planning shifts from an accuracy scaffold for weaker models to a cost saver for stronger models, with little change in accuracy") and Harness-Bench (stronger backends vary less across harnesses) predict exactly this shrinkage of scaffolding benefit, and §0 of the pack is itself the thesis that frontier models need less scaffolding — a per-prompt router is scaffolding. For three of the four routing targets (files, context-map pointers, tool calls) there is no measurement anywhere, and the vendor's own jaggedness page (jev-1.13.md, reviewed 2026-09-17) lists the properties those targets need — "Accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision", "does not count reliably", "reads dates as text", indirection "answered less reliably" — as weaknesses. A component with no baseline, no held-out delta, and a vendor sheet listing its failure modes on the exact inputs planned cannot be "core".

**Qualification:** Not the verdict, but the exact path that would revive a narrower P6: (1) build the invocation eval Joycraft lacks — real prompts from the maintainer's and colleagues' transcripts (src/telemetry.ts parsers), labeled with the intended skill or 'none', held out from any threshold tuning; (2) measure three arms on Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5: native description matching, a model-free router block/forced-eval hook, and Jev; (3) ship Jev skill routing — skills only — as per-user opt-in on the hot path only if its wrong-load minus break-rate beats the best model-free arm on the held-out set, with a kill criterion on the first month's telemetry; (4) files, context-map pointers, and tool calls stay off the hot path until each has its own eval; (5) 'core part of the product' is never available to a bring-your-own-key hosted dependency with no SLA and incidents on four of five recent days — 'optional, measured, off by default' is the ceiling the evidence supports.

**Evidence for the refutation:**
- Only routing evidence: Haiku 4.5, 182 skills, descriptions avg 54 / max 60 chars, 488 synthetic prompts by Sonnet 5, thresholds tuned in-sample, no held-out real prompts, authors admit requests are 'easier than the ones users send'; wrong-load 16.8%→7.3%, fixed 37 / broke 7, two calls per turn, 0.31s + 0.09–0.12s. — https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion.md (fetched 2026-09-24)
- Joycraft has 22 skills with 79–221-char descriptions (~3.3k total) — a different regime from the cookbook's 60-char, 182-skill roster; no skill sets disable-model-invocation. — /Users/compiler/Developer/joycraft/src/skills/*.md frontmatter (measured 2026-09-24); evidence pack §8.6, docs/research/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft-evidence.md:212
- No invocation evals exist; check.sh grades output/file only, never which skill ran — so there is no baseline native-routing error rate for Joycraft to beat. — docs/research/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft-evidence.md:212 (§8.6)
- Vendor jaggedness sheet: literal reading; adversarial content 'can move the answer'; 'Accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision'; does not count reliably; dates read as text; indirection answered less reliably; score levels 'weak in numerical calibration'. — https://docs.typesafe.ai/model-jaggedness/jev-1.13.md (last reviewed 2026-09-17, fetched 2026-09-24)
- Confidence is a spread statistic, not a calibrated probability; no ECE, reliability diagram, or accuracy-at-threshold published; 'The correct threshold values depend on your domain and the performance of the model for your use case.' — https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence.md (fetched 2026-09-24)
- Vendor positions Jev as a component inside applications the agent builds, not as a router for the coding agent; the coding-agents page makes no accuracy, latency, or reliability claims for hook use. — https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/coding-agents.md (fetched 2026-09-24)
- Scaffolding benefit shrinks with model strength: 'Planning shifts from an accuracy scaffold for weaker models to a cost saver for stronger models, with little change in accuracy.' — https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20804 (submitted 2026-09-17)
- Model-free alternative measured at 22/22 with 0 false positives (5/5 true negatives on harder set) on Sonnet 4.5 with 4 skills; Haiku classifier hook 22/22 but 4/5 false positives — an LLM judge on the hot path over-fires where a deterministic hook did not. — https://scottspence.com/posts/measuring-claude-code-skill-activation-with-sandboxed-evals (2026-02-08, fetched 2026-09-24)
- UserPromptSubmit default timeout 30s; a timed-out hook's output is discarded ('renders no decision'); a timed-out PreToolUse hook 'doesn't block the tool call ... don't count on a stalled hook to act as a gate'. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks (fetched 2026-09-24)
- API 99.827% 90-day uptime, 18 days with outages, incidents Sep 20, 21, 22 ('Elevated API latency'), 23 ('Elevated API latency', resolved Sep 24) — latency incidents are the failure mode that hits a 30s prompt hook. — https://status.typesafe.ai (fetched 2026-09-24)
- MCA: Services 'AS IS' and 'AS AVAILABLE'; TypeSafe 'may delete Customer Data at any time in its sole discretion'; 'may Process Telemetry without restriction'; Customer may not enable non-employees/non-contractors to use the Web Interface. — https://typesafe.ai/legal/mca (effective 2026-09-23, fetched 2026-09-24)
- Today the only network call in the product is a once-per-24h, 3s-deadline npm registry check; no UserPromptSubmit or http hook is installed. Hot-path Jev adds two hosted round-trips per prompt to a CLI whose sole runtime dependency is commander. — /Users/compiler/Developer/joycraft/src/update-check.ts:19-20,97,327-331; /Users/compiler/Developer/joycraft/.claude/settings.json hooks block (SessionStart + PreToolUse only); package.json:42-44
- Manifest has no ownership kind for a per-user key/config or Jev-generated routing state; kinds are vendor / create-once / config-patch only. — /Users/compiler/Developer/joycraft/src/install-manifest.ts:174

**Unverified:**
- Joycraft's actual native mis-routing rate on Fable 5.1 / Opus 5.5 with its 22 descriptions — unmeasured by anyone; the whole proposition rests on it being high.
- That any Jev routing over files, context-map pointers, or tool calls works at all — no cookbook, paper, or repo eval exists; only the vendor's own weaknesses list touches these inputs.
- The maintainer's 'insanely good' — which projects, which use (in-app judgments per the vendor's coding-agents page, or as a Claude Code router?), any before/after numbers.
- Cookbook figures on jev-1.12; whether 1.13 changed routing accuracy is not reported.
- Explicit API-key-sharing prohibition in the MCA (the Web-Interface clause and §2.2 scope were confirmed; the key clause itself was not surfaced).
- The pack's '$0.042 per million input tokens', '1,200 rpm', '64k tokens/request', 'US-only hosting' — none appear on api.md, confidence.md, or the MCA as fetched; source page not located.
- Whether a Jev adapter for the http hook really fails open under partial responses (slow-but-not-timed-out, HTTP 429/529) rather than only on hard timeout.

**On the human's position:** The maintainer wrote: "ive been using it in projects and it's insanely good and basically free, it's too good that it should be a core part of the product as it will help route what files to look at, what pointers in the context map to look at, help claude code with tool calls, I think ti will speed up development and increase quality." From my lens every load-bearing word here is an inference from n=1 with no measured delta. "Insanely good" in the maintainer's projects is an in-application use — the vendor's own coding-agents page positions Jev inside apps the agent builds, not as a router for Claude Code — so the experience does not transfer to the claimed use. "Route what files ... what pointers ... tool calls" names three targets for which no measurement exists anywhere, and the vendor's jaggedness sheet lists the required properties (accuracy under large unrelated state, counting, dates, indirection) as known weaknesses. "Basically free" is true of dollars and false of the dependency: two hosted round-trips per prompt to a service that was in incident on four of the last five days (Sep 20–23, status.typesafe.ai) and whose contract says "AS AVAILABLE" and "may delete Customer Data at any time". "Speed up development" is asserted while the mechanism adds 0.2–0.6s per prompt and, during a latency incident, up to a 30s stall before the context is discarded. The one honest hedge — "I'm open to the skeptics saying no" — is the position I move to: no, as core and on the hot path, until the baseline is measured. The maintainer's confidence is not evidence; it is the hypothesis to test, and the test costs one afternoon with `claude plugin eval` (tool_used grader) plus real prompts pulled from the existing `joycraft telemetry` transcript scanner (src/telemetry.ts).

##### Solo dev on Pi, open-weight model — qualified

**Strongest refutation:** "Core part of the product" is refuted; "an opt-in adapter that may help my model class" is not. The only routing evidence (docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion, fetched 2026-09-24) is on Haiku 4.5 over a 182-skill roster with 60-char descriptions and Sonnet-written requests the page itself calls "easier than the ones users send"; it fixed 37 and broke 7 of 488, and states a floor no router passes ("An agent given the right skill still does not always load it"). Joycraft ships 22 skills (src/skills/, 22 files) and P1 wants one hub, so the roster size the evidence assumes disappears. The one third-party Claude Code reference implementation of that cookbook (github.com/shimo4228/jev-skill-router, dated 2026-09-21) got 6/6 on scripted prompts and 3 wrong of 6 on a real session, added 0.7-1.6 s per prompt in inject mode, and its README says it is "unlikely to help a strong model as a router" because "The tokens spent on the skill listing do not go down by one." Routing to files, context-map pointers, and tool calls (the maintainer's actual pitch) has zero evidence anywhere in the pack or live docs; the only Jev ranking number is SEC-filing reranking top-1 5%->18%. Meanwhile the "free" service had eight September downtime/latency events (status.typesafe.ai, fetched 2026-09-24: Sep 2, 7, 9, 16, 19, 20, 22, 23), is "AS IS" with no SLA (typesafe.ai/legal/mca, effective Sep 23 2026), and rate limits "can change without notice" (docs.typesafe.ai/models.md). For a Pi user on Ollama (Pi docs models.md:19-27) the hot path is offline by construction, so "core" degrades to "today's behavior" for exactly the user my lens represents. A CLI whose whole runtime dependency list is `commander` (package.json:42-44) does not become a product whose default path calls a US-hosted API per prompt on one maintainer's unmeasured n=1.

**Qualification:** P6 survives only as: (1) opt-in, never default-on, gated behind a user-supplied key and an explicit local policy like update-check's; (2) shipped shadow-first on both Pi (`before_agent_start`) and Claude Code (UserPromptSubmit), logging Jev's pick beside the skill/file actually used, with inject mode enabled per harness only after the logged agreement rate on real prompts beats the zero-cost baseline (the model-free forced-eval / always-loaded router block, 22/22 on Spence's set, 100% on Vercel's 8KB index) on Joycraft's own ≤22-skill roster and on the target model class; (3) skill routing only — file, context-map, and tool-call routing stay out until any measurement exists; (4) the hard gates stay deterministic (path allowlists, exit codes), with Jev advisory, and on Pi `tool_call` blocking is allowed only for advisory-plus-confirm, never silent block; (5) the offline/local-model path (Ollama in models.json) is a first-class test case, not a degradation footnote, and the manifest gains an ownership kind for the key/policy file (src/install-manifest.ts:30 has none).

**Evidence for the refutation:**
- Routing evidence is synthetic, mid-roster-only, and self-caveated: jev-1.12, claude-haiku-4-5, 182 skills, 488 requests (315 covered), wrong loads 16.8%->7.3%, needless 9.8%->4.0%, 37 fixed / 7 broken; descriptions "truncated...to 60 characters by default"; covered requests "written by Claude Sonnet 5 from each skill's own SKILL.md" and "easier than the ones users send"; floor 2.5% wrong / 1.2% needless that "no selection method, however good, gets past". — https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion (fetched 2026-09-24)
- Only Claude Code reference build of the cookbook: shadow-first UserPromptSubmit plugin; scripted 6/6 sensible (fit 0.93-0.98); real session 3 sensible / 3 wrong, wrong cases scored 0.34-0.64; inject-mode latency 0.7-1.6 s for six decisions; 21,597 input tokens in the example call; roster 50-59 skills; README: "unlikely to help a strong model as a router" and "The tokens spent on the skill listing do not go down by one." — https://github.com/shimo4228/jev-skill-router (README dated 2026-09-21, fetched 2026-09-24)
- A model-free forced-eval hook reached 100% (22/22) with 100% (5/5) true negatives; a Haiku classifier hook hit 22/22 but only 1/5 true negatives (4 false positives). Author caveat: the 22 cases are "straightforward" and "Real usage isn't that clean." A zero-cost, offline, deterministic baseline exists and was never measured against Jev on Joycraft's roster. — https://scottspence.com/posts/measuring-claude-code-skill-activation-with-sandboxed-evals (2026-02-08, fetched 2026-09-24)
- Independent reviewer of the cookbook: "I have not independently reproduced it"; "An extra model call is another cost and another opportunity to send the work in the wrong direction"; recommends adding a selector only "when recurring selection errors justify testing one, then compare the complete workflow with and without it." — https://acdigest.substack.com/p/before-adding-more-skills-check-what (2026-09-24)
- Reliability: eight September events on api.typesafe.ai (Sep 2: 3 min; Sep 7: 3 min; Sep 9: 6 min; Sep 16: 5 min; Sep 19: 18 min; Sep 20-21: API issues + console outage; Sep 22: elevated latency 12 min; Sep 23-24: elevated latency and connection issues). 90-day API uptime 99.827%. — https://status.typesafe.ai (fetched 2026-09-24)
- Terms: "THE SERVICES AND DOCUMENTATION ARE PROVIDED 'AS IS' AND 'AS AVAILABLE'"; "TYPESAFE DOES NOT WARRANT THAT CUSTOMER'S USE OF THE SERVICES WILL BE UNINTERRUPTED OR ERROR-FREE"; use is to "include the API into one or more software applications developed and operated by Customer for the benefit of Customer's end users"; "each Customer User keeps the Access Credentials confidential and does not share them with anyone else"; "TypeSafe may Process Telemetry without restriction". Effective date Sep 23, 2026, one day before this panel. — https://typesafe.ai/legal/mca (effective 2026-09-23, fetched 2026-09-24)
- Rate limits "250,000 tokens per second / 1,200 requests per minute" and "the limits above can change without notice"; no on-prem or self-hosted option; ZDR is enterprise-only. — https://docs.typesafe.ai/models.md (fetched 2026-09-24)
- Jev "answers the question you wrote, not the one you meant"; adversarial text "can move the answer"; "Accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision" — a router fed a 3-5k-token prompt+roster+queue state is exactly that shape. — https://docs.typesafe.ai/model-jaggedness/jev-1.13.md (fetched 2026-09-24)
- Pi users can run fully local models (Ollama/LM Studio/vLLM via models.json baseUrl http://localhost:11434/v1); for them a hosted router is unreachable by design and the 'core' feature is a no-op. — node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/docs/models.md:19-27, providers.md:232
- Joycraft's runtime dependency list is exactly one package (commander). The README's only existing network call is the update check: bounded, 24h-cached, "stays quiet when offline or unavailable" (README.md:79; src/update-check.ts:97, 312-329). Per-prompt hosted calls are a category change, not an extension of that pattern. — package.json:42-44; README.md:79; src/update-check.ts:97,312-329
- No manifest ownership kind exists for a hosted-dependency configuration or key (kinds are vendor | create-once | config-patch), and today's Pi extension registers only a /joycraft-next-spec command with no hooks — a hot-path router on Pi is a new surface, not a toggle. — src/install-manifest.ts:30; .pi/extensions/joycraft-pipeline.ts:1-12,22-24
- File/context-map/tool-call routing has no evidence: the pack's only non-skill ranking datum is 75-class SEC filings (confidence >=0.9 -> 90% right, rest 40%) and reranking top-1 5%->18%; no calibration metrics published. — docs/research/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft-evidence.md:187 (section 7 item 7)

**Evidence against the refutation:**
- The one measured gain is on a mid-tier model (Haiku 4.5), which is my model class; the inverted-U (Lin et al. 2605.30621: mid-tier benefits most) predicts a Qwen/Kimi agent gains more from an external router than a frontier one. The maintainer's intuition is closer to right for my user than for the Claude Code users he tested on. — https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion; docs/research/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft-evidence.md:116
- Mechanically viable on Pi without Claude Code or MCP: `before_agent_start` "Can inject a message and/or modify the system prompt" and receives contextFiles and skills; `tool_call` can `return { block: true }`, so a Pi gate does not fail open the way a Claude Code PreToolUse timeout does. — node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/docs/extensions.md:466-483, 69-73
- Dollar cost is genuinely negligible: $0.042 per million input tokens, output free; two ~3-5k-token calls per prompt is under $0.001. Cookbook latency 0.16-0.31 s + 0.09-0.12 s per turn. — https://docs.typesafe.ai/models.md; https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion
- Inputs are not used for training ("Jev is not trained on customer requests or responses"; MCA: will not include Customer Data in training datasets without consent), so the privacy objection for a solo dev is weaker than for a shared-key design. — https://docs.typesafe.ai/models.md; https://typesafe.ai/legal/mca
- Bring-your-own-key fits the MCA better than any shared-key design: the user is the Customer, the key stays with them, and the intent already commits to fail-open degradation. — docs/intent/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft.md:31

**Citations checked:**
- Pack §7.5: status.typesafe.ai — 99.826% over 90 days, downtime on 25 days, incidents Sep 21 and 23: **misread** — Live 2026-09-24: API uptime 99.827% (holds); 17 days with downtime across api+console in the Jun 27–Sep 24 window (not 25; window drift or miscount); September incidents understated — eight events (Sep 2, 7, 9, 16, 19, 20, 22, 23), not two. The pack is too kind to TypeSafe here.

Author caveat: cases are 'straightforward'.
- Pack §7.8: jev-1.13 — reads literally; adversarial content 'can move the answer': **holds** — Verbatim at docs.typesafe.ai/model-jaggedness/jev-1.13.md; page also adds a context-rot warning ('Accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision') the pack omitted.
- Pack §7.4: MCA covers apps 'developed and operated by Customer' and forbids sharing credentials; 'as is', no SLA: **holds** — typesafe.ai/legal/mca, effective Sep 23 2026: all three phrases present verbatim. 'US-only hosting' and 'kept as long as necessary' not found in MCA or models.md — UNVERIFIED.
- Pack §7.3: $0.042/M input, output free, 1,200 rpm, 'can change without notice': **holds** — docs.typesafe.ai/models.md verbatim; also 250,000 tokens/s. typesafe.ai/pricing and docs.typesafe.ai/pricing.md both 404 (the pack did not cite them).

**Unverified:**
- 'US-only hosting' — not stated in the MCA, models.md, or api.md as fetched; source of the pack's claim unknown.
- 'Inputs kept as long as necessary' — MCA says deletion post-termination is at TypeSafe's discretion; exact retention wording not found.
- The maintainer's 'insanely good' in-project experience — n=1, no logged agreement rate, no baseline, harness and model unstated.
- Whether the MCA's 'applications developed and operated by Customer' covers a developer's own coding-agent session under their own key (plausible yes, but a legal reading I cannot make).
- Any measurement of Jev routing files, context-map pointers, or tool calls in a coding agent — none exists in the pack or in any live source I found.
- Whether Qwen/Kimi-class agents on Pi actually under-route Joycraft's 22 skills today — no invocation evals exist in the repo (pack §8.6: check.sh cannot assert which skill ran).

**On the human's position:** The maintainer wrote: "I really want this to work ive been using it in projects and it's insanely good and basically free, it's too good that it should be a core part of the product as it will help route what files to look at, what pointers in the context map to look at, help claude code with tool calls... it should be core part of the product now but I'm open to the skeptics saying no of course." Taking each clause: "basically free" is true in dollars ($0.042/M, models.md) and false in what a solo Pi dev actually pays — a second vendor account, a key in the environment, a US-hosted round trip on every prompt (0.7–1.6 s in the only Claude Code reference build), eight September incidents, "AS IS" terms rewritten the day before this panel, and nothing at all when running Ollama offline. "Route what files to look at, what pointers in the context map" has zero evidence in the pack or live docs; the maintainer is extrapolating from skill routing, and the routing datum is on a 182-skill roster he is simultaneously proposing to collapse to one hub (P1), which removes the problem Jev was measured on. "Help claude code with tool calls" is out of my lens by definition and is where the fail-open PreToolUse semantics bite. "Insanely good" in his own projects is n=1 with no baseline; the only third party who instrumented the same cookbook on Claude Code logged 3 wrong of 6 real prompts and wrote that it is unlikely to help a strong model. The irony my lens adds: the one place the evidence says Jev helps is a mid-tier agent like mine (Haiku 4.5), not the frontier setup he is testing on — so his instinct is right for the wrong user. Does my lens move his position? Yes, from "core, hot path, default when a key is present" to "opt-in Pi extension and Claude hook shipped in shadow mode, logging Jev's pick against the skill actually used, promoted to inject mode per harness only when the logged delta beats the free model-free router block on Joycraft's own roster and on real prompts." His "open to the skeptics saying no" should be taken up: not no, but not core, and not before a measurement he has never run.

##### Team lead, five engineers — refuted

**Strongest refutation:** "For anyone who brings a key" turns the router into a per-developer, per-minute fork in exactly the layer the maintainer said must stay invariant (Q1: "gates + lifecycle + artifacts fixed"). On my team, dev A (has a key) and dev B (does not) type the same prompt and land in different skills, so they produce different artifacts, and I review two shapes of output with no way to tell which path made which: Joycraft's telemetry cannot attribute a skill at all on Codex (src/telemetry.ts:404, "skill attribution is unavailable from shell strings"), and nothing in the proposal logs the Jev decision or the fallback. Dev A's own path also forks silently whenever TypeSafe wobbles, which was three of the last four days (API incidents Sep 21, 23, 24 on status.typesafe.ai, fetched 2026-09-24). The only routing evidence is a 182-skill roster shown to a Haiku 4.5 agent as 60-character lines, on requests the cookbook itself calls "easier than the ones users send"; Joycraft has 22 skills with 79 to 221-character descriptions (src/skills/*.md line 6, total about 3.3k chars) and P1 shrinks the door count further, while a model-free forced-eval hook already hit 22/22 with zero false positives. Nobody has measured Jev against that baseline on Joycraft's actual roster. Jev's own jaggedness doc says accuracy falls as unrelated state grows and that "text that argues for its own classification can move the answer"; a hot-path router is fed the raw prompt, which on a team routinely contains pasted tickets, CI logs, and PR comments. "Core" and "hot path" are the two words that fail; a logged, project-level, advisory Jev is a different proposition, and one I would accept.

**Qualification:** Would survive only if all four hold: (1) enabled per project, not per developer, so a team is all-Jev or no-Jev, with the key resolved from a committed settings.json reference to an env var and the CLI refusing to enable it when the var is missing; (2) every routing decision, confidence, and fallback written to the telemetry store so a lead can diff paths across developers; (3) an A/B on Joycraft's own 22-skill roster showing Jev beats the model-free forced-eval hook on wrong and needless loads with real prompts, not synthetic ones; (4) shipped after P1, since a hub plus few doors may remove the routing problem outright.

Three things from my lens. First, "basically free" is priced in dollars, and dollars are not what a team lead pays; I pay in review variance, and the clause "for anyone who brings a key" is the exact mechanism that creates it: five engineers, some keyed and some not, walking different paths through a lifecycle Q1 says must be fixed, with telemetry that cannot even name the skill on Codex (src/telemetry.ts:404). Second, the maintainer's own list of wins is mostly files, context-map pointers, research, and panels, which are the off-hot-path advisory uses the lead recommended and r7 rated lowest-risk; only "help claude code with tool calls" needs the hot path, and that is the use with the weakest evidence and the strongest adversarial exposure. Third, "insanely good" is one super-user on his own projects with no logged error rate; the Q2 answer ("if I can get it to work best for me, we can easily get it for others") is the assumption my lens exists to test, and it fails here, because a solo user never sees the cross-developer divergence a team lead reviews daily. My lens moves the position from per-user opt-in to per-project all-or-none, from core hot path to logged advisory, and from "ship because it feels good" to "ship after it beats the free 22/22 hook on Joycraft's own 22 skills." The maintainer said he is open to a no; on the stated shape, this is one.

##### Evidence auditor — refuted

**Strongest refutation:** P6 as stated ("core part of the product," routing prompts to skills, files, context-map pointers, and tool calls on every prompt) rests on exactly one measurement plus one anecdote, and neither transfers. The one measurement is TypeSafe's own skill_suggestion cookbook, and the live page adds four facts the pack omitted: the published run used jev-1.12 rendered 2026-07-31 (not the 1.13 model whose jaggedness page is dated 2026-09-17); the 488-request test set is proprietary (requests.json not published); the "covered" requests were written by Claude Sonnet 5 from each skill's own SKILL.md, so the labels are trustworthy but "the requests are easier than the ones users send"; and the cookbook's own conclusion scopes the pattern to "when an agent of yours carries a large roster" — 182 skills, agent Haiku 4.5. Joycraft has 22 skills (one hub after P1), targets Fable/Opus/Astra, and the pack's §0 thesis is that frontier models need less scaffolding — so the 16.8%→7.3% delta was measured on the wrong roster size, the wrong agent, the wrong Jev version, and requests the vendor calls easier than real. There is zero measurement anywhere in the pack, the repo, or TypeSafe's docs for routing files, context-map pointers, or tool calls; TypeSafe's own coding-agents page (docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/coding-agents.md, 2026-09-24) positions Jev for "an app or agent you're building" and states it "is not a drop-in replacement for the LLM behind Claude Code," offering no hook-on-every-prompt guidance. The anecdote ("insanely good and basically free" in the maintainer's own projects) has no artifact in this repo: grep for jev/typesafe across src/, templates/, scripts/ returns nothing. Meanwhile the operational citations all hold or are worse than stated: MCA updated 2026-09-23 restricts use to applications "developed and operated by Customer for the benefit of Customer's end users" and forbids enabling access by anyone "who is not an employee or independent contractor of Customer"; "AS IS" and "AS AVAILABLE," no SLA; telemetry processed "without restriction"; status page shows incidents Sep 20–21, Sep 22, and Sep 23–24 (three, not two, in the last five days); and the hooks doc says a UserPromptSubmit hook "blocks model processing until it completes, a stuck hook stalls the session" (default 30 s) before its context is discarded — so "degrades to today's behavior" costs up to the timeout on every prompt during the very incidents the status page records. A model-free forced-eval hook measured 22/22 with 0/5 false positives (Scott Spence, 2026-02-08) and has never been run against Joycraft's roster. A core product feature cannot rest on a non-transferable vendor cookbook plus an unmeasured anecdote.

**Qualification:** Could return as qualified only if all of: (a) an eval on Joycraft's actual roster (22 skills or the post-P1 hub) with Fable 5.1/Opus 5.5 as the agent, on requests not authored from the skills' own descriptions, shows Jev beating the model-free forced-eval hook (which measured 22/22, 0/5 false positives) by a stated margin; (b) the hook is opt-in with a per-prompt timeout of ≤2 s, not the 30 s default, so 'degrades to today's behavior' costs at most 2 s during incidents; (c) TypeSafe confirms in writing that a user running Joycraft's hook with their own key falls within 'developed and operated by Customer' under the 2026-09-23 MCA; (d) file/pointer/tool-call routing stays out of scope until each has its own measurement. Absent (a) and (c), the proposition has no verified source to stand on.
