**Skeptic disagreements:**
- Verdict split: team-lead ruled 'qualified', novice, ai-researcher and evidence-auditor ruled 'refuted'. Their qualifications converge on the same residue (per-user, uncommitted, presentation-only), so the split is over whether that residue counts as P11 surviving.
- Self-assessment reliability: team-lead says weak (McIntosh et al. 2022, r=0.43-0.47) and evidence-auditor adds novices misjudge quality (Cloude et al. LAK 2024); evidence-auditor and novice counter that a single programming-experience self-estimate correlates well (Feigenspan et al. 2012, rho=0.539; Siegmund et al.) and that the pack's 'unreliable' angle is overstated. Novice explicitly says its refutation does not rest on this point.
- Where the residue lives: team-lead wants it in Joycraft's docs/.joycraft/local/ (cross-harness, Joycraft-owned); evidence-auditor says Claude Code output styles in .claude/settings.local.json already ship it and Joycraft should contribute only a pointer (Claude-only; no verified equivalent on Codex/Pi/omp/Copilot); ai-researcher wants a BMAD-style config.user.toml value shipped only behind a measured delta; novice wants no stored profile at all and per-session inference from how the human talks, with the unread 'User expertise' brief line as the home.
- Infer-from-behavior: novice's qualification endorses per-session inference; team-lead and ai-researcher reject behavior inference (arXiv 2608.10319: pooled generic skills beat personalized; joycraft-optimize.md:70: per-machine counts stop being evidence past ~3 contributors); evidence-auditor found no source either way and notes joycraft telemetry records reads, not skill signals.
- Whether a vocabulary fork is worth anything: ai-researcher reads arXiv 2502.18685 as showing the expert register is fine regardless of user level, cutting against even a vocabulary residue; team-lead and evidence-auditor treat plainer explanation as a legitimate rendering preference; team-lead adds that a vocabulary fork on shared artifacts violates STE rule 10.
- Shapiro citation label: novice marks it 'holds' with a note that the novice/no-CS framing extends past the source; team-lead and evidence-auditor mark it 'misread'. Same substance, different label.
- Whether a mixed-skill audience exists: all four say unverified; novice and evidence-auditor treat Q2's 'mixed skill' as asserted not shown; team-lead and ai-researcher grant Q7's novice lens as some pull toward P11.
- Which mechanism absorbs the skill gap: novice and evidence-auditor read the maintainer's 'becomes a non issue' as the harness doing more; team-lead says the default altitude should be the super-user's set per project; ai-researcher says treat any fork as an eval question (delta on held-out tasks) not a setup question.

**Citation problems:**
- Dan Shapiro 'Five Levels' (pack §0, §9 P11; docs/guides/levels.md): misread. The post's levels are collaboration modes for developers; it has no non-programmer tier, so 'novice ... no CS background = Levels 1-2' is the pack's gloss. levels.md:17 'Most developers plateau at Level 2' also does not match the source, which puts '90% of AI-native developers' at Level 2 and says 'almost everyone tops out' at Level 3.
- Skill-creator post (pack §4.6): the implied URL claude.com/blog/skill-creator returns 404; live page is claude.com/blog/improving-skill-creator-test-measure-and-refine-agent-skills (2026-03-03). Live wording is softer: 'may become less necessary as models improve' and encoded-preference skills are 'more durable', not 'persist'; preferences are framed as 'your team's process', not per-user.
- gstack (pack §5.5): the setup profile is per-MODEL (reads Codex config.toml), not per-user, and the README tells the user to add the 'Skill routing' CLAUDE.md section manually rather than setup writing it (evidence-auditor, fetched live).
- McIntosh et al. 2022 at royalsocietypublishing.org: HTTP 403 (dead for the panel); verified via PMC mirror PMC9727674.
- Pack §8.6 '10 of 22 skills exceed 200 lines': 12 by optimize's own wc -l method (evidence-auditor). Not P11-specific but a pack error.
- SkillsBench (pack §4.1) cites the superseded v1 (+16.2pp, 86 tasks); current revision (2026-06-14) reports 87 tasks, +16.6pp, and the abstract no longer mentions the self-generated condition (ai-researcher).
- Pack §4 inference 'per-user regeneration risks the ACE-style collapse' extends an online-adaptation-without-feedback result to static profiles; that step is the pack's, not the paper's (evidence-auditor).
- Anthropic 'How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills' (2026-01-29, 52 devs, -17%): numbers from secondary search hits only; primary not fetched by any skeptic.
- Feigenspan et al. 2012 rho=0.539 and Cloude et al. LAK 2024: secondary snippets only; Springer redirected to auth, ACM returned 403.
- Atharva Vaidya architecture-defense practice and its 'requires a CS background' constraint (pack §0): personal report, no URL, no artifact; the entire positive case for P11 rests on it.

**What would change the ruling:** Any one of: (1) a named daily Joycraft user who cannot read a diff, with a specific gate where they churn or abandon, which would make the novice path a real segment rather than an asserted one; (2) instrumenting the existing `User expertise` brief field and showing that its value changes any downstream outcome (gate pass rate, rework, abandonment) across several features; (3) a measured delta on a held-out task set (per `claude plugin eval` or Joycraft's own evals) showing that a self-declared altitude improves shippability or reduces abandonment versus one path with STE explanation; (4) evidence that the P10 architecture-defense gate fails for non-CS users even when explained at their level, rather than being merely uncomfortable, which would justify user-keyed gating of P10 specifically; (5) a per-user, uncommitted instruction surface appearing on Codex, Pi, omp, or Copilot, which would make a cross-harness per-user profile implementable without new Joycraft machinery. Evidence that self-assessment is more reliable than the pack implies would NOT change the ruling, because the ruling rests on the frame contradiction, the missing home, and the absent demand, not on unreliability.

**Human position moved?** Yes, moved, and in the direction of the human's own words. Section 10 has no direct P11 answer; the fork is the human's proposed mechanism in §0 ("setup asks for the user's technical background, and that forks the abstraction level"), framed to serve the Atharva architecture-defense practice for practitioners while sparing 'novice users'. The panel moves that position on four points of evidence. First, the human's Q1 ("Gates + lifecycle + artifacts fixed; process prose generated") and Q2 ("one path"; "as this system gets ... more driven by the harness this becomes a non issue") already contradict the mechanism: a fork of gates and artifacts by user is what Q1 fixes, and 'one path' is the opposite of two altitudes. Second, the novice segment is asserted, not shown: no named user cannot read a diff, Joycraft's own levels guide targets Levels 3-4, and the Shapiro framework cited for 'novice' has no non-programmer tier. Third, the repo has run the experiment quietly: the brief's `User expertise` field has existed with zero consumers, and the only shipped precedent (BMAD) dropped its tailoring six weeks ago. Fourth, the measured data (Bing Copilot: expert register is fine regardless of user level; arXiv 2608.10319: pooled beats personalized) says the practitioner altitude should be the default for everyone. Where the human lands after the panel: keep P10 as a gate for all users and let the agent do the explaining in STE; set any altitude per project in AGENTS.md next to the Execution Profile; treat per-user explanation depth as an uncommitted rendering preference, built only when a named user needs it; and pursue 'teach people' through content and a simpler harness, as the human himself predicted, not through a setup question.

#### Skeptics

##### Novice vibe coder — refuted

**Strongest refutation:** The proposition adds the one thing that makes me quit — another setup question I cannot answer — to serve a user who does not exist in the confirmed frame. Shapiro's Levels 1–2 are developers ("You're writing the important stuff, but you offload specific, discrete tasks to your AI intern"; "pairing with the AI like a colleague"); the post has no non-programmer tier, so "no CS background" and "Level 1–2" are two different axes that §0 line 22 conflates. Joycraft's own levels.md:22-23 says its job is Levels 3–4; the README (line 45) starts me at `npm install -g joycraft` and (line 160) tells me "you approve the brief and the specs, the agent executes with TDD". The maintainer's Q2 names the users: himself and ~15 daily-driver colleagues on "one path". Nobody named cannot read a diff. Meanwhile today's setup already asks me which harnesses (`claude, codex, pi, copilot, omp` — harness.ts:78-84), then four execution-profile questions per harness ("Use swarms for decompose?", "Model", "Effort" — execution-profile.ts:173-188), then shared/private git tracking, then auto-memory (setup-walkthrough.md:36-45); tune adds 3–5 risk questions plus git autonomy (tuning.md:9,20); new-feature asks "smoke test budget? lockdown mode desired?" (new-feature.md:104). A "what is your technical background?" question is one more I will answer wrong ("intermediate, I shipped an app with Cursor"), and because the fork "gates which gates run", my wrong answer silently changes what I get with no way for me to notice. Joycraft already captured this exact self-assessment once — the brief template's "**User expertise:** [comfortable / learning / needs guidance]" (new-feature.md:181) — and zero skills, templates, or tests read it (grep of src/skills, src/templates, tests: one hit, the template line). The demand for a fork never materialized in the product's own skills. And because Q1 fixes gates, lifecycle, artifacts, STE and the TDD loop as invariant, the only thing left for my "altitude" to change is vocabulary and hiding the P10 code-defense gate — vocabulary the model already adapts per reader without a stored profile (Fable 5 guide: "The vocabulary you built up while working is yours, not theirs; leave it behind"). Finally, the product's promise is to move me from Level 1 to Level 4; a background snapshot taken at setup is wrong within weeks if the product works, and unlike tune (re-scored every run) nothing re-scores it.

**Qualification:** Not P11, but what could survive from it: no setup question and no stored profile; the agent infers reader mode per session from how the human talks (the existing unread 'User expertise' line is the natural home) and changes presentation only — which evidence an artifact shows (screenshot vs diff), never which gates run or how many. Even that is worth building only after one named user who cannot read a diff is using Joycraft daily.

- Joycraft's own levels table gives Level 1 the role "-" and states "Joycraft's job is to make you excellent at Levels 3-4"; the README audience approves briefs and specs and starts with npm install. — /Users/compiler/Developer/joycraft/docs/guides/levels.md:14-26; /Users/compiler/Developer/joycraft/README.md:45,160
- The brief template already carries a self-assessed expertise field, "User expertise: [comfortable / learning / needs guidance]", and nothing consumes it: grep over src/skills/*.md, src/templates/, tests/ returns only the template line. — /Users/compiler/Developer/joycraft/src/skills/joycraft-new-feature.md:181 (sole hit)
- Init already asks a novice four questions it cannot answer per harness (swarms for decompose, swarms for implement, model, effort) and a harness-selection question listing five harness names; the walkthrough lists four setup questions before the tool is usable, then tune adds 3–5 risk questions plus a git-autonomy question. — /Users/compiler/Developer/joycraft/src/execution-profile.ts:173-188; /Users/compiler/Developer/joycraft/src/harness.ts:78-84; /Users/compiler/Developer/joycraft/docs/guides/setup-walkthrough.md:36-45; /Users/compiler/Developer/joycraft/docs/guides/tuning.md:9,20

##### Team lead, five engineers — qualified

**Strongest refutation:** On a team, "altitude" is a property of the project, not the person. Every artifact the fork would change is committed and shared: AGENTS.md and the Execution Profile are create-once, team-owned, ONE_HOME data (src/update-inventory.ts:233-262; src/execution-profile.ts:9-12 "team-shared data the human owns"), docs/.joycraft/manifest.json is tracked (git ls-files), and checkpoint pages, decision rows, and specs land in the repo. If a per-user profile gates which gates run (P9 visuals vs P10 code-level defense) or how much ceremony applies, then the same repo accumulates features that passed different gates depending on who typed the prompt. The lead cannot assume any feature passed the architecture defense, review load rises because artifact shape varies by author, and the decision log becomes inconsistent by author. That is an advisory gate by another name, which the maintainer's own Q4 answer ("gates that cannot be overridden") and Helix ("gates are blocking, never advisory", pack §0) both reject. The input to the fork is also weak: self-estimates track measured ability at r = 0.43-0.47 (McIntosh et al., Royal Society Open Science 2022, n=151), and the one empirical study of per-developer personalization found "small and inconsistent improvements" versus "the largest and most consistent gains" from generic skills pooled across developers (arXiv 2608.10319, 2026-08-10, 206 sessions, 13 developers). Anthropic's skill-creator post frames encoded-preference skills as sequencing "according to your team's process", not the individual's (claude.com, 2026-03-03). Finally the vocabulary half collides with the maintainer's Q1 invariant: the STE output contract governs all human-facing output and rule 10 says "one word for one concept" (src/templates/reference/output-style.md:6-9 and rule 10); STE in pragmatic mode is already the single-register answer for readers of mixed ability, so a per-user vocabulary fork forks the invariant. There is no cross-harness per-user home either: CLAUDE.local.md counts as a CLAUDE.md and stops AGENTS.md loading on Claude Code (code.claude.com/docs/en/memory, table rows for AGENTS.md; fetched 2026-09-24), Codex reads AGENTS.md with no per-user project instruction layer (pack §3 table), and Joycraft's only gitignored per-user-per-project home is docs/.joycraft/local/ (.gitignore:15), which today holds one presentation flag, autoOpen (src/skills/joycraft-tune.md:89).

**Qualification:** P11 survives only as a per-user rendering preference: vocabulary and explanation depth in chat and in the human-facing parts of artifacts, stored per user and gitignored under docs/.joycraft/local/, overridable per session, and inside the STE contract (plainer sentences, not a second term set). Under that condition the fork changes nothing that is committed: which gates run, how much ceremony applies, what a checkpoint asks, and what lands in specs, decision rows, and PR bodies stay identical for every author and are set per project in AGENTS.md by the repo owner. If the profile gates any gate or ceremony, or if it writes into any committed artifact, the proposition is refuted for any project with more than one author.

**On the human's position:** The maintainer's Q2 answer is "Solo practitioners of mixed skill; maintainer first as super-user, colleagues second, one path", and the rationale adds that the colleagues are "across different size teams" and that "as this system gets much easier ... more driven by the harness this becomes a non issue really." Two of the maintainer's own words refute P11 as written. "One path" is the opposite of a per-user fork of gates and ceremony. And "this becomes a non issue" is an argument that the skill gap is closed by the harness doing more, not by asking the user how skilled they are. The Q1 rationale names STE a "biggest win": STE exists so that one register serves a tired or inexperienced reader and an expert alike, and its rule 10 forbids rotating vocabulary within a document, so a per-user vocabulary fork on shared artifacts contradicts the invariant the maintainer wants fixed. My lens moves the position in one direction only: harder toward one path. The altitude must be set per project by whoever owns the repo (the lead), in the committed AGENTS.md next to the Execution Profile, identical for every author; the default altitude is the super-user's, because that is who the product is tuned for. What a novice on the team gets is not fewer gates but the same gates with plainer explanation in the human channel, and that is a rendering preference that belongs in docs/.joycraft/local/, never a gate switch. The maintainer's design should also reject "infer from behavior": the one study on it found generic pooled skills beat personalized ones, and the repo's own optimize skill already documents that per-machine behavioral counts stop being evidence past three contributors.

##### AI researcher — refuted

**Strongest refutation:** P11 has no measurement behind it and borrows its plausibility from studies about a different variable. Every "adapt to capability" result in the pack — the harness ablation (planning +11.6pp for Nemotron-3 30B, −2.0/−0.4pp for 550B and Mistral-Medium at ~30% lower cost) and Lin et al.'s inverted-U — measures the agent's pass rate as a function of the backbone MODEL with no human in the loop; transferring that to human expertise is a category error. The one measurement that does concern user expertise (Bing Copilot, 25k conversations, arXiv 2502.18685) found the agent answering at proficient/expert level "correlates with positive user experience regardless of the user's level of expertise," while answering BELOW the user's level hurts, most on complex tasks — so the fork's only reachable failure (a practitioner routed down to the novice altitude) is the measured harm, and the "benefit" (a novice routed down) is a direction the data says is unnecessary. The gate input itself is unreliable in exactly this population: METR's RCT (16 experienced devs, 246 issues, 2025-07-10) had developers predict +24%, measure −19%, and still believe +20% afterward; Anthropic's 52-developer RCT (2026-01-29) shows the novice who would most need the fork is the one whose comprehension is being eroded by delegation, i.e. the level drifts under the tool. The only harness that shipped this exact knob — BMAD's `user_skill_level` (beginner/intermediate/expert, per-user config) — removed it from its Build skill in v6.11.0 on 2026-08-09 ("Build drops its `user_name` greeting and `user_skill_level` tailoring"). And Joycraft has quietly run this experiment already: the brief template captures `User expertise: [comfortable / learning / needs guidance]` (src/skills/joycraft-new-feature.md:181) and nothing in src/skills, src/*.ts, templates, or tests consumes it — a self-declared expertise field with zero downstream effect and zero telemetry. Finally, the proposition contradicts the human's own frame: Q1 fixes "Gates + lifecycle + artifacts" as the invariant, and P11 varies which gates run and what artifacts show per user.

**Qualification:** Survives only as a per-user, uncommitted, revocable explanation-depth preference that changes no gate, no artifact, and no committed file — i.e. BMAD's pre-v6.11 `user_skill_level` in config.user.toml — and only if it is shipped behind a measured Δ on a held-out task set. That is not "forks the abstraction level"; it is a verbosity setting the only precedent already dropped.

**On the human's position:** Section 10 never states a position on P11 directly; the fork is the lead's mechanism for the maintainer's Atharva observation in §0 ("requires a CS background, so it is useless for Joycraft's novice users"). The maintainer's own words cut against P11 twice. Q1: the invariant is "Gates + lifecycle + artifacts fixed; process prose generated" — P11 varies which gates run (P9 visuals vs P10 code defense) and what artifacts show, so it forks the very thing Q1 declares invariant; if only prose varies, the proposition collapses to vocabulary, which frontier models already adapt without a profile and which the Bing data says is fine at the expert register. Q2: "Me truly first as I am the super user... then I'll make content etc.. around into teach people... as this system gets much easier house and more driven by the harness this becomes a non issue really" — one path, maintainer first, novices served by content and by the harness getting simpler, not by a second altitude. The only pull toward P11 is Q7's added novice-vibe-coder lens. My lens moves the human's position by removing a false premise: the maintainer treats a background question as a reliable input, and the one population measured (experienced developers, METR) mis-assesses by ~39pp even after direct experience. The measured, cheap replacement is behavioral: Joycraft already has `joycraft telemetry` and the unread `User expertise` field; instrument whether that field ever changes an outcome before building a fork on it. Concretely: keep gates and artifacts one path, let the agent explain more when asked, and treat any per-user fork as an eval question (Δ on a held-out task set, à la `claude plugin eval`) rather than a setup question.

##### Evidence auditor — refuted

**Strongest refutation:** P11 has no evidence base. Its only support in the pack is one uncited anecdote from a colleague who does not use Joycraft (evidence pack §0, "Architecture-defense session"); none of the nine external sources I re-fetched shows any harness forking on a user's self-declared technical background — gstack forks per MODEL (reads config.toml, github.com/garrytan/gstack README, fetched 2026-09-24), Helix adapts per accumulated approved work and "makes no mention" of engineer skill or per-user profiles (shopify.engineering/helix, 2026-09-21), and Anthropic's skill-creator post ties durable skills to "your team's process," not to individuals (claude.com/blog/improving-skill-creator, 2026-03-03). The one framework P11 uses to define "novice" is misread: Dan Shapiro's levels are collaboration modes, not skill levels; the post puts "90% of 'AI-native' developers" at Level 2 and says "almost everyone tops out" at Level 3 (danshapiro.com, 2026-01-23), so "Levels 1-2 = novice market" is not in the source (Joycraft's own docs/guides/levels.md:17 says "Most developers plateau at Level 2," which also does not match the source). The fork P11 wants — "which gates run, how much ceremony, and what artifacts show" — is exactly what the human fixed as the invariant in Q1 ("Gates + lifecycle + artifacts fixed; process prose generated"), and the vocabulary residue already exists per-user outside Joycraft: Claude Code output styles (Explanatory: "You're getting to know a codebase"; Learning: hands-on practice) stored in .claude/settings.local.json, which Claude Code keeps out of git (code.claude.com/docs/en/output-styles and /settings, fetched 2026-09-24). What is left for Joycraft to build is either already shipped by the host or contradicts the human's own invariant.

**Qualification:** The only residue that survives: a per-user, non-committed vocabulary/explanation setting (Claude Code output style or an equivalent in .claude/settings.local.json) that changes how results are explained and never which gates run, how much ceremony, or what artifacts contain. That residue is already shipped by Claude Code and has no verified equivalent on Codex, Pi, omp, or Copilot, so Joycraft's contribution would be a one-line pointer, not a profile captured at setup.

**Evidence for the refutation:**
- Setup captures nothing about the user today: grep of src/skills/joycraft-setup.md for background|novice|experience|level|profile|vocab returns zero lines; init's only interactive questions are harness, gitignore profile, and the per-harness execution profile (swarms, model, effort). — src/skills/joycraft-setup.md (grep, 2026-09-24); src/execution-profile.ts:163-175
- The execution profile is explicitly per-harness, team-shared, human-owned data with ONE_HOME in AGENTS.md — the module comment says 'the profile is team-shared data the human owns and hand-edits'; it is not a per-user surface and cannot be made one without a second home. — src/execution-profile.ts:8-11, 20-26; AGENTS.md:177-183
- The manifest has no per-user file kind: ManifestFileKind = 'vendor' | 'create-once' | 'config-patch'. The human-facing vocabulary contract (docs/templates/reference/output-style.md, STE) is a committed vendor-owned file replaced on every update, so a per-user vocabulary fork would either edit a vendor file (replaced + backed up each release) or need new machinery. — src/install-manifest.ts:39; docs/.joycraft/manifest.json:116-121 (kind: vendor, v0.7.17); docs/templates/reference/output-style.md:1-30
- Shapiro's levels are ways of working with AI, not measures of technical skill; the post says '90% of AI-native developers are living right now' at Level 2 and 'almost everyone tops out here' at Level 3. P11's 'Levels 1-2 = novice' mapping and levels.md's 'Most developers plateau at Level 2' are not in the source. — https://www.danshapiro.com/blog/2026/01/the-five-levels-from-spicy-autocomplete-to-the-software-factory/ (2026-01-23, fetched 2026-09-24); docs/guides/levels.md:17,25
- gstack's profile fork is per-model, not per-user: 'For Codex, setup reads the top-level model from ${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}/config.toml and generates the matching behavioral profile.' The README 'contains no features for per-user profiling, technical assessment, or adaptive difficulty levels.' — https://github.com/garrytan/gstack README (fetched 2026-09-24)
- Helix adapts on accumulated approved work — 'As approved code and feedback accumulate, later checkpoints can run with less oversight' — and makes 'no mention' of adapting to engineer skill level, background, vocabulary, or per-user profiles. Its gates are blocking for everyone. — https://shopify.engineering/helix (Talha Naqvi, 2026-09-21, fetched 2026-09-24)
- Claude Code already ships per-user altitude knobs: Explanatory ('You're getting to know a codebase') and Learning ('hands-on coding practice') output styles, saved to .claude/settings.local.json ('You, in this one project only'; Claude Code adds it to global git excludes) or ~/.claude/settings.json. The doc also warns a style 'doesn't guarantee that something always happens' and 'styles don't change how [subagents] respond' — so a vocabulary-only fork is instruction-only and never reaches fresh-context verifiers. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/output-styles and https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings (fetched 2026-09-24)
- Self-assessment is least reliable for the segment P11 targets: novices 'inaccurately monitor the quality of their work and their peers' work' (hard-easy effect: overplace on easy tasks, underplace on hard ones). — Cloude, Kumar, Baker, Fouh, LAK 2024, https://doi.org/10.1145/3636555.3636848 (abstract via researchportal.tuni.fi and search snippet; ACM full text returned 403)
- The human's Q1 invariant fixes 'Gates + lifecycle + artifacts'; P11 forks 'which gates run' and 'what the artifacts show.' The proposition contradicts the frame the panel is told to argue inside. — docs/research/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft-evidence.md §10 Q1 row

**Evidence against the refutation:**
- A single self-estimate question is the best cheap predictor of programmer performance: 'On a scale from 1 to 10, how do you estimate your programming experience?' correlated ρ=0.539 with performance on 10 comprehension tasks (best of all background questions). So 'self-assessed skill is unreliable' is overstated for practitioners. — Feigenspan, Kästner, Liebig, Apel, Hanenberg, 'Measuring programming experience', ICPC 2012 (number via search snippet from Siegmund et al. follow-up; primary PDF not fetched)
- Per-user local overrides are a sanctioned pattern on Claude Code: 'Each teammate can still override it for themselves in their own .claude/settings.local.json, so personal exceptions don't need a commit.' A Claude-only, gitignored altitude setting would not collide with committed artifacts. — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings (fetched 2026-09-24)
- The maintainer reports fifteen daily-driver colleagues 'across different size teams' and wants content to 'teach people' — a real mixed-skill audience exists. — docs/research/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft-evidence.md §10 Q2 row

**Citations checked:**
- Dan Shapiro, 'The Five Levels' (danshapiro.com/blog/2026/01/...), cited in P11 as 'Levels 1-2 vs 3-4' and in docs/guides/levels.md: **misread** — Source exists (2026-01-23). Levels are collaboration modes, not skill; '90% of AI-native developers' at Level 2; 'almost everyone tops out' at Level 3. P11's novice=Levels 1-2 mapping and levels.md's 'Most developers plateau at Level 2' are not in the source.
- gstack README: 'setup reads the model and generates the matching behavioral profile' and writes a 'Skill routing' section into CLAUDE.md (pack §5.5): **misread** — Profile sentence holds but is per-MODEL (Codex config.toml). The README tells the user to add the CLAUDE.md section manually; it is not written by setup. No per-user profiling anywhere.
- Shopify Helix (shopify.engineering/helix, 2026-09-21): feedback 'recorded in memory to improve every checkpoint that follows'; autonomy grows with approved work (pack §0): **holds** — Verbatim: 'Helix records it in memory to improve every checkpoint that follows' and 'As approved code and feedback accumulate, later checkpoints can run with less oversight.' No per-user or skill-level adaptation in the article.
- Anthropic skill-creator post (claude.com/blog, 2026-03-03): capability-uplift skills fade, encoded-preference skills persist (pack §4.6): **holds** — Date and both quotes hold ('may become less necessary as models improve'; 'more durable'). Frames preferences as 'your team's process', not per-user.
- ACE paper arXiv 2510.04618: playbook 18,282→122 tokens, accuracy 66.7→57.1, baseline 63.7; 'depends critically on feedback quality' (pack §4.2): **holds** — All numbers verbatim in v3 body (not in abstract). Note the pack's inference 'per-user regeneration risks ACE-style collapse' extends an online-adaptation-without-feedback result to static profiles; that step is the pack's, not the paper's.
- Claude Code output styles doc (code.claude.com/docs/en/output-styles) — new evidence I brought, not in the pack: **holds** — Explanatory/Learning styles; stored in .claude/settings.local.json or ~/.claude/settings.json; instruction-only; do not apply to subagents.
- Claude Code settings doc (code.claude.com/docs/en/settings) — settings.local.json is per-user and kept out of git: **holds** — 'You, in this one project only'; Claude Code adds **/.claude/settings.local.json to global git excludes when it creates the file.
- Feigenspan et al. ICPC 2012, self-estimate ρ=0.539: **not-checked** — Number taken from a secondary snippet (Siegmund et al. summary); ResearchGate/Springer primaries not fetched (Springer redirected to auth).
- Cloude et al. LAK 2024, novices inaccurately monitor quality: **not-checked** — Abstract confirmed via Tampere research portal snippet; ACM full text returned HTTP 403.
- Pack numbers vs repo: 22 skills, 5,573 lines, 141 {{skill_prefix}} occurrences, '10 of 22 skills exceed 200 lines': **misread** — 22 ✓, 5,573 ✓ (wc -l src/skills/*.md), 141 ✓. But 12 skills exceed 200 lines by optimize's own wc -l method (src/skills/joycraft-optimize.md:110), not 10.

**Unverified:**
- Atharva Vaidya's architecture-defense practice and its 'requires a CS background' constraint (pack §0) — personal report, no URL, no artifact; the entire positive case for P11 rests on it.
- Feigenspan/Siegmund ρ=0.539 at the primary source (secondary snippet only).
- Whether Codex, Pi, omp, or Copilot have any per-user (non-committed) instruction surface analogous to Claude Code's settings.local.json/output styles — not in the pack; not checked.
- Whether the fifteen colleagues are actually novices (Levels 1-2 in Joycraft's sense) or practitioners — no data in the pack; the Q2 answer says 'mixed skill' without evidence.
- Whether behavior-inferred skill (from telemetry) beats self-report — no source in the pack or found; `joycraft telemetry` (src/telemetry.ts) records reads, not skill signals.

**On the human's position:** The human's Q2 words: "Me truly first as I am the super user of this product… 15 colleagues all of use it daily driver, across different size teams… if I can get it to work best for me, we can easily get it for others… as this system gets much easier house and more driven by the harness this becomes a non issue really" — confirmed as "maintainer first as the super-user, colleagues second, ONE path." And Q1: "Gates + lifecycle + artifacts fixed; process prose generated," naming STE as a "biggest win." Read literally, the human has already voted against P11 twice: one path, not two altitudes; gates and artifacts fixed, not forked by user; and STE (docs/templates/reference/output-style.md, vendor-owned) already fixes the human-facing vocabulary for everyone, which is the exact thing a vocabulary fork would vary. The human's own prediction — that the novice/practitioner gap "becomes a non issue" once the harness drives more — is the strongest argument against building a background profile now, and it needs no evidence I could not find. My lens moves the position in one direction only: it strengthens it. The human's "mixed skill" audience claim is unverified (no data on the fifteen colleagues), the framework Joycraft cites for novice-vs-practitioner is misread at the source, and the only per-user altitude mechanism verified live (Claude Code output styles, per-user, gitignored) already exists outside Joycraft. If the maintainer still wants an altitude knob, the evidence supports at most: point users at the host's per-user output style, and never let any per-user setting change which gates run.
